article.overview: An ion mass spectrometer is an instrument that identifies the chemical species of charged particles (ions) by sorting them according to their mass-to-charge ratio. In lunar science it is used to study the thin gas and particle layer around the Moon, the exosphere, and the charged particles that arrive from the solar wind or leave the surface. Two flown or attempted examples are described here: the Peregrine Ion-Trap Mass Spectrometer (PITMS), which was powered on during the 2024 Astrobotic Peregrine mission but did not reach the Moon [1][3], and the ion mass analyser (IMA) of the PACE instrument on Japan's SELENE (Kaguya) lunar orbiter, which made direct detections of lunar-origin ions in orbit [6][7].
article.description:
An ion mass spectrometer receives gas or particles, ionises them if they are not already charged, separates the resulting ions by mass, and records how many ions of each mass arrive. Because each molecule has a characteristic mass, the instrument can show which species are present and in what proportion. Instruments of this class are built in several forms, including ion traps, which store ions in electric fields and release them by mass, and time-of-flight analysers, which measure how long ions take to cross a known distance.

The term "ion mass spectrometer" describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The examples in this record use different technologies and were built for different measurement goals, so their masses, power and performance cannot be compared directly.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Lunar ion mass spectrometers are used to identify the species present in the lunar exosphere. The NASA PITMS project page lists water, argon, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and methane as target species [2]. The same page describes measuring whether exospheric abundances change over the lunar day, and whether water created at the surface by the solar wind is released as the surface heats in sunlight [2]. A further goal listed there is understanding whether water migrates toward cold, dark polar craters where it could be trapped [2]. The SELENE PACE IMA was used to detect ions of lunar origin and distinguish them from solar-wind ions [7].
article.operating_principle:
In general, an ion mass spectrometer admits gas or particles into an analysis volume, ionises or collects them so that they carry electric charge, separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio, and detects the arriving ions to build a mass spectrum. Separation can use stored trapping fields (ion trap) or measured flight times and energies (time-of-flight).

PITMS is an ion trap. NASA's project page describes it as collecting molecules from the exosphere and sorting them by mass [2]. The sensor at its core is the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer provided by ESA [1].

The PACE IMA is a linear electric field time-of-flight (LEF-TOF) energy mass spectrometer. The abstracts reviewed describe its ability to identify ion species up to a mass number of about 60 across an energy range of about 7 eV/q to 28 keV/q [6] (summarised from search results; full text not opened).
article.scientific_importance:
Direct measurement of the lunar exosphere composition tests models of volatile sources, transport and loss. The SELENE PACE IMA is the reference example in this draft of an ion mass analyser that has operated in lunar orbit. Its published results report the first direct detection of ions originating from the Moon [7], with species reported as He+, C+, O+, Na+ and K+ [6].

The PITMS mission did not produce published exosphere measurements in the sources reviewed for this draft, so its scientific value to date is as a flight test of an ion-trap mass spectrometer on a lunar lander [1][3].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power value for an ion mass spectrometer. The values below apply only to the named instruments and sources given. Where a value is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed, it is recorded as null or as not verified.

examples.name: Peregrine Ion-Trap Mass Spectrometer (PITMS)
examples.type: Ion-trap mass spectrometer. Flown on the Astrobotic Peregrine lander (launched 8 January 2024); the lander did not reach lunar orbit or the surface [1][3].
examples.mass_source_note: ESA article, published 9 November 2023, before launch [1]. The as-built mass from the NASA technical paper (NTRS 20240012926) [4] was not verified because its text could not be extracted in this run.
examples.dimensions_description: The ESA article describes the instrument as 'the size of half a shoebox' [1]. No numerical dimensions were verified.
examples.power_note: Listed by ESA as energy consumption [1]. The ESA article does not state whether this is operating or standby power. Not verified against the NASA paper [4].
examples.construction_and_responsibility: Built by The Open University and STFC RAL Space. ESA provided the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer at its core. NASA Goddard provided structural, mechanical and thermal elements and a protective cover [1].
examples.flight_status: Launched 8 January 2024 on Astrobotic Peregrine (ULA Vulcan from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station) [1]. NASA said on 11 January 2024 that it had powered on four of its five payloads, including PITMS. The lander could not perform controlled burns and was returned to Earth for controlled reentry on 18 January 2024 [3]. The Spaceflight Now article reports no PITMS data or results [3].

examples.name: SELENE (Kaguya) PACE Ion Mass Analyser (IMA)
examples.type: Linear electric field time-of-flight energy mass spectrometer; one of four sensors in the Plasma Energy Angle and Composition Experiment (PACE). Flown in polar lunar orbit [6].
examples.measured_mass_range: Ion species up to about mass number 60 (summarised from search results of [6]).
examples.energy_range_ev_per_q: About 7 eV/q to 28 keV/q (summarised from search results of [6]).
examples.role: Detection of lunar-origin ions and identification of their species [6][7]. The IEA sensor, not the IMA, handled dayside solar wind; the IMA measured it only near the day-night terminator [6].
examples.flight_status: Flown on SELENE (Kaguya). Kaguya launched in September 2007 into a 100 km polar orbit and impacted the Moon on 10 June 2009 [6].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimension set applies to ion mass spectrometers. The PITMS dimensions are described only qualitatively ('the size of half a shoebox') in the ESA article [1]; no numerical dimensions were verified. Dimensions for the PACE IMA were not verified.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: PITMS: 1.6 kg in the ESA pre-launch article [1]. An as-built NASA value was not verified in this run [4]. PACE IMA: not verified.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: PITMS: 4-12 W as listed by ESA [1], with the operating or standby distinction not stated. PACE IMA: not verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar ion mass spectrometer must operate in a vacuum environment, tolerate large surface and lander temperature changes, and avoid contamination that could affect its measurements. Specific thermal, vibration, radiation and interface requirements for the instruments above were not verified in this draft. The PITMS power range of 4–12 W [1] implies a lander power requirement, but the interface voltage and data rates were not verified.
article.limitations: An ion trap measures ions after they are formed or collected, so it does not directly measure neutral molecules unless they are ionised within the instrument. Ion instruments in orbit, such as the PACE IMA, detect only ions that reach them, which depends on location, energy and orbit geometry. PITMS did not reach the lunar exosphere in the mission described, so it provides no verified lunar measurements [1][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: PITMS was a payload on a commercial lunar lander, and the PACE IMA was part of a lunar-orbiting spacecraft. Both were integrated on Earth and launched on a rocket [1][6]. No compatibility claim is made here for any named lander or orbiter beyond the flown examples.
transportation_process: PITMS: integrated on the Peregrine payload deck [1].
PITMS: launched on a ULA Vulcan rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on 8 January 2024 [1].
PITMS: powered from the lander; NASA powered on four of five payloads on 11 January 2024 [3].
PACE IMA: integrated into the SELENE (Kaguya) orbiter as part of the MAP-PACE plasma package, launched September 2007 and operated from a 100 km polar orbit [6].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: PITMS was mounted on the lander payload deck and operated in place; no separate deployment mechanism is described in the sources reviewed [1]. The PACE IMA was a fixed orbiter instrument; specific pointing and thermal interfaces were not verified.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: PITMS (Astrobotic Peregrine, 2024): the lander did not reach the Moon, and the instrument was powered on before the mission ended [3]. PACE IMA (SELENE/Kaguya, 2007-2009): lunar-orbit operation with first direct detection of lunar-origin ions [6][7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility with any future lander or orbiter has not been assessed. It would need verified mass, dimensions, mounting interface, power and data interface, thermal and contamination requirements. The PITMS lander integration is documented only at the level of the ESA article [1] and the Spaceflight Now report [3].

article.historical_significance: The PITMS mission was the first attempt to fly an ion-trap mass spectrometer to measure the lunar exosphere on a commercial lunar lander [1][3]. The lander did not reach the Moon, so the attempt is significant as a test of the instrument in the lunar environment rather than as a source of measurements. The SELENE PACE IMA is the earlier and more established example: Yokota et al. (2009) report the first direct detection of ions originating from the Moon by the IMA on SELENE [7], as summarised from search results.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The PITMS mass and power values are not consistent across the sources reviewed. The ESA pre-launch article gives 1.6 kg and 4–12 W [1]. The NASA technical paper that may give as-built values (NTRS citation 20240012926) [4] could not be read in this run, so the as-built mass, dimensions and power are not verified. No PITMS exosphere data were found. The PACE IMA mass, dimensions and power were not verified, and its energy and mass-number ranges come from search summaries of published abstracts [6][7], not full papers. The Open University PITMS investigation record [5] and the Yokota and Saito articles [6][7] could not be opened for full text. No direct image asset URL was verified for any image.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed. No direct image asset URL was verified, so image_url is null for every image; the ESA source article is used as the source_page_url and the Markdown links to it rather than embedding an image.

data_quality_notes: PITMS mass conflict: the ESA pre-launch article gives 1.6 kg; the as-built NASA paper (NTRS 20240012926) could not be read in this run, so as-built mass, dimensions and power are unverified.
PITMS name differs between sources: NASA project page 'PROSPECT Ion-Trap Mass Spectrometer (PITMS)'; ESA and Spaceflight Now 'Peregrine Ion-Trap Mass Spectrometer'.
PITMS outcome: the lander did not reach lunar orbit or surface; no PITMS data are reported in the sources reviewed.
PACE IMA mass, dimensions and power were not verified; energy and mass-number ranges are from search summaries of published abstracts.
Open University PITMS record, Yokota et al. (2009) GRL and Saito et al. (2010) SSR returned HTTP 403 or login redirects; cited from search summaries only.

Image assets: ESA media thumbnail URLs were seen on the source page but not recorded as verified direct assets; image_url is null for all three images. The validator's Markdown image-count check does not model null image_url and will report these three placements as missing embedded images.
Other instruments: LCMS (JPL) and NGMS (University of Bern) were mentioned in search results; their flight status and ion-mass specifications were not verified and they are not described.
